title: Without going out the door
hookLine: without going out the door, know the world (Tao Te Ching 47)

lines: FAR AWAY, TO FIGURE IT OUT.
cards: A suitcase sits by the door, half packed. The plan is a trip far away to finally figure things out: a mountain, a coastline, a city where everything will be different. Some people take that trip and come home changed.
Some come home with the same questions in a different suitcase. Chapter forty-seven of the Tao Te Ching has something to say to the half-packed bag, and it begins with a door that never opens.

teach.b: First, the claim. In James Legge's translation, chapter forty-seven opens: "Without going outside his door, one understands (all that takes place) under the sky."
Without looking out of the window, it goes on, one sees the way of heaven. Second, the warning.

teach.h: THE FARTHER OUT, THE LESS YOU KNOW.
teach.b: Legge again: "The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows." Notice his little bracket, from himself. He reads the going out as going away from yourself, not only as travel.
Third, what the chapter is not saying.
It doesn't forbid journeys or call seeing the world useless. Its point is about where understanding comes from.
The sage, it says, knows without traveling, names things without seeing them, and gets things done without forcing.
Knowing, in this chapter, happens close to home: in attention, in stillness, in the life right in front of you.
Fourth, the room you're in. It's easy to think the answer is somewhere else: a new city, a new job, a retreat across the world, the next video.
Sometimes it is. But chapter forty-seven points at the kitchen, the window, the street you walk every day, the people already in the house.
A cup of tea drunk slowly at your own table can teach something a long flight can't. Before going out the door to look for the world, look at the room you're in.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-seven as a reason to look for insight in stillness and in ordinary home life, rather than only in travel or new experiences.

games.q: what does “without going out the door” mean?
o: a rule against ever traveling far from home
a fear of the world that waits outside
understanding the world from close at hand

p: one sees the way of heaven

s: its point is where understanding comes from, not a ban on journeys.
Legge adds the words 'from himself' in brackets
he reads going out as going away from yourself.
the chapter says the sage gets things done by forcing
it says the sage gets things done without forcing.

games.q: you're stuck on a big question and planning a trip far away to sort it out. what does chapter forty-seven suggest first?
o: go farther; the answer is out there.
look closely at the life and room you're in.
ask everyone you meet on the way.
games.why: the chapter says that without going out the door one understands the world, and the farther one goes out, the less one knows.

practice: Stay exactly where you are, and look slowly around the room, or the car, or the bench, as if you'd traveled a long way to see it: the light on one wall, a sound from outside, the texture of whatever you're sitting on.
Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward, to the breath and the weight of your body. Nothing to go out and get.
